utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This is case number IT-97-25-T, the Prosecution versus Krnojelac.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: We apologise for the late start. Perhaps a very good illustration of why the United Nations should never run Tribunals. Through no fault of any of the participants, the meeting started 35 minutes late. But it was an important one, and Judge Mumba and I had to attend it. So we're very sorry for the late start. We'll sit through until 11.30, as we originally stated and then resume at 12.00 and then go through until 1.30. Now, Mr. Bakrac, you're cross-examining.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I would like to just ask the usher to help me, please. Because of the ELMO and the screen, I can't see the witness at all. So I find this a bit inconvenient.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Good morning, sir. Can you hear me? I said good morning. Good morning. What is the reason why you haven't said "Good morning"?

utterances.speaker: FWS-73 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was told that my answers should come a bit late because of the interpretation.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Sir, you said in your statements to the Prosecutor that contact with you can be established through AID in Sarajevo. Can you tell me what that is?

utterances.speaker: FWS-73 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you explain that to me? I'm not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: The abbreviation is AID Sarajevo. Is that an organisation? If so, what kind of organisation?

utterances.speaker: FWS-73 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not aware of any organisation.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Is it necessary for me to show you your statement? Would you like to look at it? Would you like to read what it says?

utterances.speaker: FWS-73 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would kindly ask the usher to help. Could he please show the witness his statement dated the 28th of June 1997. 139A is its identification number. Can he please leave the -- Can he please read the text that follows after the words "address."

utterances.speaker: FWS-73 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Have I signed this?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would again ask the usher for his assistance. I found the English version.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, we can supply it. We have it here, Mr. Bakrac.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I found it. I found it, yes. I do apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: This is the English version that you're handing him which has been signed.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is marked ID-139.

utterances.speaker: FWS-73 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what's wrong about this.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: The English version that you signed, it also says, "Contact through AID in Sarajevo."

utterances.speaker: FWS-73 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was in Sarajevo then. I was questioned by a group of judges from Canada in relation to another person.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: I understand that, sir. But contact with you is established through AID in Sarajevo. What kind of organisation is that? What is that?

utterances.speaker: FWS-73 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that in Sarajevo there are judges who come from all parts of the world. So as for this organisation, AID, I've never heard of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Sir, why are you lying to us here?

utterances.speaker: FWS-73 [Resumed]
utterances.text: So now I'm lying to you? Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: The "contact through AID Sarajevo," that's obviously something that the investigator wrote, and to tell the witness that he's lying because he cannot explain this abbreviation, I think that's going far over the top.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Well, Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff, I can only say that if that had been inserted by the investigator, it should have been made clear. You can't blame counsel if somebody has signed a document that he may be contacted through a particular acronym, that he would not have known what it is. I agree with you the suggestion that somebody is lying is beyond what is reasonable in the circumstance, and I think the witness reacted quite reasonably in the way he did. Mistaken or asking for an explanation before you assert that somebody is lying is usually the way to cross-examine properly. But I have to say that the way in which the Prosecution takes its statements leads to this sort of problem. The investigator has no job -- it is no part of his duties to add things for somebody else to accept. It could be a note on it somewhere, "This witness" -- by the investigator, "This witness may be reached through AID Sarajevo." Do you know what AID Sarajevo is?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think that's the police in Sarajevo. And very often investigators -- the investigators are supposed to not put down the address of the witness in this witness first page, and therefore this investigator, for reasons I don't know, made this note, probably meant for further contacts. I think it's the police in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: It may be a good idea, just so that it's cleaned up once and for all, if the investigator is asked and we can be told later on just who this group is. But Mr. Bakrac, I think you've spent enough time on this issue. Let's get on to something which is important.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I agree, Your Honour, but please allow me to put about two more questions to the witness in relation to this, because the explanation is highly illogical.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Are you saying that contact with you can be established through judges from all over the world? That's what you said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Oh, now, look, Mr. Bakrac, if there is one thing we have learnt by listening to this witness is that he does not answer questions. He tells us what he wants to say. I'm not saying that in criticism of him, but it's very clear that that's the situation. Now, you are going to provoke more problems than it is worth by trying to get him to keep doing this and to explain why he's doing it. Some witnesses are like that. Let's go to the facts of this case that we really have to worry about. If you think that there is something in AID which is sinister, that you can take advantage of, perhaps you could tell me who is AID Sarajevo. Do you know?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I know, Your Honour -- or, rather, I know what I heard. I haven't checked this out. I haven't got documents, so I can't stand behind this, but this is an organisation that deals with persons that might testify in court, so I don't really want to stand by these words unless I have their statute, their rules, their articles of foundation, whatever. However, on the basis of what I heard in Bosnia, AID Sarajevo, that is an organisation that is in constant contact with potential witnesses concerning crimes that were committed against Muslims. And that is what many citizens of Bosnia and Herzegovina are aware of, and I'm sure that this witness is aware of that as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Let's assume that that is so. Where does it get us?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, you said yourself a few minutes ago that the way in which this witness answers questions shows certain things. And I think that it is important for the Defence to show the Chamber how this witness speaks about certain matters. After all, the examination-in-chief has shown that this witness does not really have any details. He speaks in general terms about names that are being repeated here, and he doesn't have a very good memory concerning dates and other particular details. When he claims that some persons have been killed, he doesn't say that they went missing, although he never saw any of this, things like that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: I think all of that is perfectly apparent on the transcript and you can make what you can of it, but what I am concerned about is you can pursue a line that he is pro-Muslim and anti-Serb if you wish. I would have thought that's fairly obvious already from his answers throughout the whole of his evidence. I don't say that that's something which we will take into account to his discredit. I'm afraid that both sides seem to have the same problem in this benighted country. But the point is made. I don't think you need to labour that point. That's why I'm asking you please let's go to the facts of the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Yes, Your Honour. I would just like to ask the usher to return these documents to me because I may need them during the course of my further examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Sir, could you please tell me whether you had an apartment or whether you lived in a house?

utterances.speaker: FWS-73 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had a house, and I lived in it.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Is that house in Cohodar Mahala?

utterances.speaker: FWS-73 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is in the old centre of the town of Foca.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: So it's not in Cohodar Mahala?

utterances.speaker: FWS-73 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it's not in Cohodar Mahala.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: And what about the (redacted) or, rather, your business establishment? I beg your pardon.

utterances.speaker: FWS-73 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The business establishment is three kilometres away from my private house.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Thank you. Tell me, please, sir, did you obtain any weapons before the war broke out?

utterances.speaker: FWS-73 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Before the war broke out, and I never believed that this would happen, I did not even think of anything like that. I had a business establishment, and I didn't even have a pistol. And I could have had a pistol, according to regulations, otherwise.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: On the 9th of April, were some kind of roadblocks set up in Donje Polje?

utterances.speaker: FWS-73 [Resumed]
utterances.text: As for roadblocks, I don't know about any of them. However, I do know that masses and masses of Serbs passed by my house, and I was wondering what all of that was about.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: You don't know about the roadblocks by the cafe Bor?

utterances.speaker: FWS-73 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about any kind of roadblocks, either from the Serb or the Muslim side.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Sir, on the 15th of October, 1994, did you give a statement to the security centre in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: FWS-73 [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I arrived from the notorious camp in which I was for two and a half years, I gave some statements, but until the present day, I've been wondering how I can speak at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Could you please be so kind as to explain to me what does that exactly mean? How can you say that you've been wondering how you can speak at all?

utterances.speaker: FWS-73 [Resumed]
utterances.text: After all these atrocities that I personally saw, that I experienced, after slaughters, torchings, killings, I don't know how come I'm alive after all these horrors.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: That is to say that you are not quite certain that everything you've said here as a witness is true?

utterances.speaker: FWS-73 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Everything I said here as a witness, except that I don't remember dates and that I do not remember last names with 100 per cent certainty because some last names are similar and these persons are from the surroundings of Foca, so it is only in that area that I see that I'm not 100 per cent sure, and I explained this to the Honourable Court. However, all the rest I've been saying is true.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: When did you have a stroke, sir?

utterances.speaker: FWS-73 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had a stroke after I got out of prison. Everything was -- I started eating normally, I started living normally, and a few years ago, I had a stroke when I started having a normal life. I guess that my organism could not deal with all of that, my blood vessels, things like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: When did you suffer a stroke?

utterances.speaker: FWS-73 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot remember any date specifically.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: So since your stroke, you haven't been able to remember even the year when you suffered your stroke?

utterances.speaker: FWS-73 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can say that I had this stroke about three years ago, two to three years ago. I can't say for sure. I can't say the date for sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Can you give us the exact year?

utterances.speaker: FWS-73 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it was 1998/1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Did you remember better before your stroke or has the stroke refreshed your memory?

utterances.speaker: FWS-73 [Resumed]
utterances.text: My memory, both before the stroke and after the stroke -- except that after the stroke I also got some kind of freshness which I cannot describe to you, actually, because I'm not a medical person.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Sir, on the 15th of October, 1994, before your stroke, you gave a statement to the security station in Sarajevo. Did you give this statement at all?

utterances.speaker: FWS-73 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In order to help the interpreters, I'm going to read a brief passage slowly, but I'm going to mention where it's from. It is ID 140, statement to the security station in Sarajevo, on the 15th of October, 1994. I'm going to start from the second sentence from the very beginning.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: "However, since the situation was tense because of the events from the Focatrans scandal and because of the strange relations between the Muslims and the Serbs, some Muslims, including myself, armed themselves."

utterances.speaker: FWS-73 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Are you asking me to give an answer in relation to that?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Do you want me to show you the signature on this document?

utterances.speaker: FWS-73 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Had I been armed, that moment I would have been beaten, battered and killed, even if I had a pistol with a licence. I think that I've said everything by having said that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: So you were not saying the truth in the security centre in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: FWS-73 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The investigator, the first time and the second time, and also the first time I told you when I was questioned in camp about -- given all these horrors of war, I signed everything. I didn't even look at what he wrote down. I'm telling you the same thing now. In the security centre in Sarajevo, when I got out of the notorious camp, tears were flowing all the time. The Chetnik laws are well-known. Everybody who had something, even with a permit, was killed if that was found. That's my answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. In the next sentence, you said, "In Foca, the war events started on the 9th of April, 1992, when barricades were set up outside the Bor catering establishment. These barricades were put up by Muslims among whom I recognised a man called Subasic, nicknamed Rana, a man called Lojo and others whose names I do not remember." You said just now that you are not aware of any kind of barricades.

utterances.speaker: FWS-73 [Resumed]
utterances.text: My answer to this is the following: During the trial, I have said -- during the trial before this Honourable Court, I have said -- or, rather, whatever I said is 100 per cent true. As for the examination in Sarajevo, after I came from the notorious camp, I'm talking about myself, and I'm also talking about what had happened to us. We were beaten, we were totally distraught. So whoever wrote all of this could have written it at his own discretion and I could have signed it. The fact that they say that I was armed, and I have been repeating what happened to people who even had a pistol with a licence, a permit; they disappeared.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Do you know that all these people who disappeared had pistols or Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. weapons?

utterances.speaker: FWS-73 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. They were told so. It seems here that I was boasting that I had had some weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: How come you didn't go missing?

utterances.speaker: FWS-73 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, because in this text, it says that I had weapons too. In the text, that's what it says. And that is incredible because I never had any weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Did you read the statement you gave in the KP Dom?

utterances.speaker: FWS-73 [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I got this statement, I was so afraid that I would be mistreated, and others as well, I didn't even dare look at it. If that statement said, "Sign this, and this will be your death warrant," I would have signed it.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: How come you know that that statement did not say that you had weapons?

utterances.speaker: FWS-73 [Resumed]
utterances.text: They could have written whatever they wanted to. It was their affair. They could write whatever they wanted to write and there was no control whatsoever. So they wrote whatever they wanted to write.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: In the statement you gave to the security centre in Sarajevo it says that Esad Taljanovic took this statement. Can you guess what ethnicity he is?

utterances.speaker: FWS-73 [Resumed]
utterances.text: You said Esad. That can be a Muslim only, but then on the other hand, his last name can be Serb or Croat. So I have no idea who he is or what he is.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Esad Taljanovic can be a Serb, as far as you're concerned?

utterances.speaker: FWS-73 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am saying in terms of his surname. Esad is a Muslim name whereas Taljanovic can be a Serb or a Muslim or a Croat last name. I personally am not really interested in that, I mean surnames and names, whatever it might be.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Yes, sir, we know that. We have seen that from your testimony here. However, what about this security centre in Sarajevo? Did it belong to Republika Srpska or to the federation of Bosnia-Herzegovina at the time when you gave this statement?

utterances.speaker: FWS-73 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not involved in politics before and I was not involved in politics when I came to Sarajevo, and even now that I came to a foreign country, I am not involved in politics at all, so I didn't really pay any attention to all of this, having gone through all this suffering.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: May I remind you, sir, to pause before you commence your answer? As you said earlier this morning, it is important and it is of great help to the translators if you do so. You didn't for the last two answers that you gave. Yes, Mr. Bakrac.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: What I'm asking you, sir, is not politics; it's a fact. Are you trying to tell me that you had no idea after you were exchanged and came to Sarajevo who Sarajevo did belong -- or, rather, who the Centre of Public Security in Sarajevo belonged to? Is that what you're trying to tell us?

utterances.speaker: FWS-73 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am trying to tell you that when I left the infamous camp in Foca, when I gleaned some freedom, I wasn't interested in either this or that. All I was interested in was find my children, find a slice of bread, to recover.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: But, sir, that is not the answer to my question. I asked you do you know who the Public Security Centre in Sarajevo belonged to at the time when you arrived there, and when you gave a statement there on the 15th of October, 1994?

utterances.speaker: FWS-73 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I repeat, once again, as regards politics, I know nothing about it. But what I want to say is this: When I arrived in Sarajevo, I saw Olivara Visotski [phoen], sister of the brother of a deputy from the infamous camp at Kula, Visotski [phoen]. I saw brother who was in Sarajevo and his brother is in the camp in Foca in the mechanical shop as the shop -- as the chief guard. I saw Trajan Krsmanovic. That is all men I knew. I saw both Serb and Croat and Muslim people, and I thought I had reached freedom and that was all, nothing else.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. I won't go into this. I think I understand from what you tell me. It's all become clear. So it is not correct what you said in the statement that the Muslims who had set up a barricade to Donje Polje did not allow anyone, any of the staff of KP Dom to pass through? That is not true either, is it?

utterances.speaker: FWS-73 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I told this Honourable Court in my yesterday's testimony. When they saw a group of Muslims being slaughtered, torched, then in Donje Polje, they -- they were defending. And I repeat as the statement says that my neighbour personally told me, "Phooey! We thought it was all dug in," but nothing like that ever happened. That is what I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: So it is true that in that same statement, you said that you had heard stories from people who were close to sources that Foca had such armaments, that nobody could take it, and from the -- and from this statement it seems to you that it fell on the very first day of the Chetnik attack.

utterances.speaker: FWS-73 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I repeat today what I told the Honourable Court yesterday in my testimony, when the extremist Serbs said that if anyone votes for a sovereign Bosnia-Herzegovina that his throat would be slit and his house burnt down. And this story spread around the town. So some, in order to put an end to these tall stories, some said, "Ha! We're stronger. We're better." I said it yesterday. I don't see why I have to repeat that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: But, sir, does it seem logical to you that the public security centre in Sarajevo writes then that Muslims put up roadblocks, that they're arming themselves, that you were armed, without your having told them so? Why should the public security centre in Sarajevo, which is part of the Muslim-Croat Federation there, why would they write such a thing?

utterances.speaker: FWS-73 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I hear what you are telling me and I understand you very well, but I repeat once again, in my business outlet, in my house, from needle to the thread everything was searched and carried away. Had anything been found and I had been driven to the camp -- I was driven to the camp in those same clothes that I was wearing that day.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, may I interrupt the witness and ask him to answer my questions if I can, or if I cannot, then I think he should say so in order to save time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Mr. Bakrac, he clearly has not answered your question - you're right about that - but your question was an argumentative one: "Don't you think it's illogical, the explanation you're given?" Your duty as a cross-examiner is to raise the issue that he has signed a document in which there is an inconsistent statement. You've asked him to explain it. He's explained it by saying that he was prepared to sign anything that was put in front of him and he didn't really read it at all. Now, you can test that, if you like, but just arguing with him as to whether it is logical is not testing it, it's just arguing. And if I may say so, you're not getting very far on that issue. He's made his position very clear and we accept it or reject it as it comes at the end of the case. But you've certainly raised the issue. Now, let's get on to the next statement that you want to bring him into conflict with.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. I do agree. That is what I intended to do, to just try to move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Are you familiar with the name Saja Sahimpasic?

utterances.speaker: FWS-73 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Are you aware that he was the president of the Muslim Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: FWS-73 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me answer you like this: Saja Sahimpasic and his neighbours, when they saw, I repeat, the taking over of the radio station and of the post office - they're both in the town centre - with his neighbours he tried to resist the infamous Chetniks.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Did you know Saja well before the war?

utterances.speaker: FWS-73 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Any Focan of the Bosnian Serb and Croat ethnicity knew very well, every one of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Yesterday, sir, you told us during examination-in-chief that your wife was kept for one, two, maybe three days in the KP Dom; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: FWS-73 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct. Or let me tell you again. In all that plight, when I didn't know where I was -- and I do not know whether to tell the Court that I love my wife better than I love myself. And I didn't know where my wife was.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: In this statement to the Prosecutor's Office, you said that, "My wife and I were taken in a car to the KP Dom. My wife was kept there only a few hours."

utterances.speaker: FWS-73 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Before the Honourable Court I will repeat again. Whether a few hours or a day or two, be that as it may, but she left quickly, and I shall never deny that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: You said you came upon paramilitary formations in the KP Dom. Were they standing guard there?

utterances.speaker: FWS-73 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The KP Dom paramilitary units came for a day or two, perhaps, when we were already there, and all our locals were the ones who had arrested us, who were at the gate, and who took us in.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: In your statement to the OTP in 1995, you said, "In the prison I saw the soldiers, members of paramilitary units such as Arkan's men, Seselj's men, and the White Eagles. They acted there as guards but they were also helping the prison guards who were locals."

utterances.speaker: FWS-73 [Resumed]
utterances.text: My answer to this is yesterday I stated before this Honourable Court, and I repeat it today, the miscreants, thieves, murderers who came from the nearby Serbia, from the nearby Montenegro, had been invited by a -- local miscreants, and their cooperation meant slaughter, burn, and take the booty. They stayed there for a short while and they left.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Sir, would you know if during the war that you are talking about, were there any casualties, any losses on the Serbs or any victims on the Serb side caused by, inflicted by Muslims? Are you aware of any camps that were kept by Muslims for captured Serbs?

utterances.speaker: FWS-73 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Are you referring to Foca?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: I'm referring to Bosnia in general.

utterances.speaker: FWS-73 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've already said that I am not interested at all in politics or any other knowledge.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: So you're not interested in victims. You're not aware of any Serb victims that were -- camps where Serbs were kept; is that correct??

utterances.speaker: FWS-73 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'll tell you --

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: No. Tell me if this is correct or if it is not correct.

utterances.speaker: FWS-73 [Resumed]
utterances.text: What?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Are you aware of camps in which the Muslims kept Serbs? Are you aware of crimes committed against Serbs or are you not aware of them or you indifferent to this, as you put it?

utterances.speaker: FWS-73 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is not that I'm indifferent to it. I appreciate every life like my own. But what I'm saying is: That is politics. All camps which started, the whole world knows about them. So I don't -- there is no need for me to explain anything to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: But I'd like to hear whether you would call those Muslims miscreants, thieves and --

utterances.speaker: FWS-73 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'd call the same name to every man who does anything like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Sir, in the statement that you gave to OTP, on page 4, the end of the third passage, you say the following: "Savo Todovic, who was representing military authorities there, all orders for torture and killing came through him. I learned that from a person whose identity I do not wish to reveal." Is this statement correct?

utterances.speaker: FWS-73 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is correct, and I learned that when criminals began to come to the camp who committed crimes amongst themselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: What criminals do you mean?

utterances.speaker: FWS-73 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I mean criminals on the Serb side, who -- and I repeat, and I pointed out to the Honourable Court yesterday, when they kill, after they've killed and torched, and then about the booty, who will get more, who will get less, they began to fight among themselves and they killed some of them. I did have an opportunity to meet some of them in Foca. One of them was a salesman in Foca and we also heard it on the news.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Is it correct, sir, that in your second statement to the OTP, 1997, you said the following: "In relation to what I said in my previous statement about Savo Todovic, a Serb who worked in the KP Dom told me that Savo Todovic was responsible for the execution of the orders of the SDS leadership in the KP Dom. Those SDS leaders wielded control over both military and civilian functions." Is this what you stated then?

utterances.speaker: FWS-73 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I will put it like this: Not one miscreant who held an office had to be a member of the SDS.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: But what I'm asking you, sir, is: Did you make this statement, the one that I've just read out to you?

utterances.speaker: FWS-73 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did state that, but alongside this reasoning.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Did you also state that you had learned that Todovic issued orders to Rasevic, a guard commander, about who was to be taken out for beating?

utterances.speaker: FWS-73 [Resumed]
utterances.text: My statement, it was phrased like this: I go to enterprise --

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: I'm asking you if you stated this or if you didn't state it?

utterances.speaker: FWS-73 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did but -- it wasn't taken into account what the truth is because what it said, what I thought was the real truth and I stated it.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: In your last statement of 1998, and you were asked about this, you said that Savo Todovic -- that you thought that Savo Todovic had even more authority than Krnojelac. Is that the result of all these statements that you made here?

utterances.speaker: FWS-73 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I repeat: Savo Todovic was subordinate to the previous one. Or let me put it this way: If you give a fool a stick, then you understand it all, if you get my meaning.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: I do, sir. Thank you. Yesterday, when you described your first meeting with Mr. Krnojelac, you said you asked him, "What's this?" And that he told you that you would be interrogated in a few days' time and then released. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: FWS-73 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: In these statements to the OTP, the first one, in 1995, you said that you had seen Krnojelac after arriving in the KP Dom, and then you said, "I asked him, 'What is going on here?' And he merely shrugged his shoulders." In your second -- no, in your last statement of 1998, you also said the following: "When I first saw Krnojelac in the prison, I was taken by surprise. He was standing at the gate. I asked him, 'What's this?' But he did not reply." Did he or didn't he reply to you? In one statement you said that he shrugged his shoulders and said nothing. Today you tell us that he told you what I mentioned already to you.

utterances.speaker: FWS-73 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I say that when -- when I -- when my wife and I were brought to the camp, we knew Krnojelac personally and we asked him. We knew him. We didn't know those others. And the one who was guard I used to meet in the street at times. And I asked and he didn't reply. He merely shrugged his shoulders. He behaved indifferently, if you get my meaning, something like, "Well, it has to be this way," something, something like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Well, did he reply or didn't he?

utterances.speaker: FWS-73 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, with this lifting of the shoulders, and in that nightmare it seemed to me that he'd answered it and with this shrugging of the shoulders, I understood that he meant, "Well, this will be over too." That's what I understood with all that fear.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. You knew Krnojelac before the war, did you?

utterances.speaker: FWS-73 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I knew him before the war but -- and perhaps we sat at the same table in a cafe, in Cisija's cafe. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: And was he ever in your business outlet?

utterances.speaker: FWS-73 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, perhaps once or twice. I can't remember exactly because he wasn't the one who patronised coffee shops and restaurants much.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Did he perhaps teach any of your sons?

utterances.speaker: FWS-73 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he taught my son. He taught mathematics.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Did you communicate with him in that regard, with your son's teacher?

utterances.speaker: FWS-73 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I never went to see him to get some information.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Nor your wife?

utterances.speaker: FWS-73 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't really say. I can't remember about my wife, but I never went to see him.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Sir, if we leave aside the position that you claim he had in the KP Dom, what is your impression -- what was your impression about Krnojelac before the war conflict broke out?

utterances.speaker: FWS-73 [Resumed]
utterances.text: My impression about Krnojelac as a man before the war conflict was normal.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Did I understand you correctly yesterday when you said that when you used to see Krnojelac in the KP Dom, did he shake hands with you?

utterances.speaker: FWS-73 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Personally, I can say, as regards Krnojelac, that he has culture and good manners, and that culture and good manners, I was surprised that it never came to the surface when this Krnojelac said -- decided to send a person like Savo Todovic to communicate with Mustafa Rasevic and -- Raskadic and others.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Tell me, you used to -- you said that you used to see him in civilian clothes, in a former uniform without any markings. Did you ever see him in a blue, prison uniform?

utterances.speaker: FWS-73 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The prison uniform was worn only by guards because they had inherited it from the communist, socialist system, and so they walked around in that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. And I will read out to you what you said to the OTP in 1998: "First time I saw Krnojelac in the prison, I was taken by surprise. In the beginning, he wore civilian clothes, and later on, I would see him only in a KP Dom uniform."

utterances.speaker: FWS-73 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The answer you know. I repeat again. All that was left over from the KP Dom, they put on. And that also applied to Savo Todovic. That is those olive-grey/green, sheep skin and all that. Whatever they could pick up, they wore, because other people's clothes somehow looked better on you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Sir, are you aware that in the early days of the conflict, Mr. Milorad Krnojelac's house burned down?

utterances.speaker: FWS-73 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am aware that in the early days of the war, Krnojelac's house burnt down. That is the upper part.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: What happened?

utterances.speaker: FWS-73 [Resumed]
utterances.text: During the shelling, the roof of the forest ranger's house went ablaze and a part of the building went ablaze and, I also heard that Mr. Krnojelac's house went up in flames. But how and why, I do not know, but I've heard about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Yesterday, when you described the incidents with Cedic and Isanovic, when did that happen? Did it happen on the same day that you were brought to the KP Dom?

utterances.speaker: FWS-73 [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I was brought to the KP Dom, I say once again I don't know the dates. All I know is that it was the beginning so a list would be brought to those miscreants, that is the locals would bring the list, and these miscreants would take the list and then beat. That was in the beginning.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: I was about to remind you that you told us that. Now I shall tell you what you said in the statement to the OTP.

utterances.speaker: FWS-73 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just a moment. May I ask the Honourable Court, may I -- I need to go to the toilet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: That's all right. We are about to take a break anyway. We will resume again at 12.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Sir, if you have any medical problem that you need to attend to, don't hesitate to ask and we will excuse you while you do so. Yes, Mr. Bakrac.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Sir, before the break I put a question to you in relation to the Cedic-Isanovic incident. I did not ask you to tell me precisely which day this was. Was this the first day when you arrived in the KP Dom? And also, is what you said correct, that is, that the guards of the KP Dom brought the list of those two?

utterances.speaker: FWS-73 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I pointed out to the Honourable Court, when I was speaking yesterday, that I do not remember a day or two, but at any rate, this was the beginning, when people were first being brought in. After a few days, perhaps even a month had elapsed, but during that month, that is when it happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Is it correct that it is the guard of the KP Dom who brought the list?

utterances.speaker: FWS-73 [Resumed]
utterances.text: These extremist forces that were from the area around Uzice, the area around Scepan Polje, these neighbouring lands, they didn't know anyone. So as people would say, they wouldn't even know how to pronounce this last name. Whenever they got these lists, I mean, I'm speaking personally about Cedic, Isanovic, they would always say "Isanovic," because a list had been brought. "Cedic, you should go out into the hall."

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Sir, I'm going to read to you what you said in your first statement in 1995: "On that first day when I arrived in the KP Dom, two men who were detained with me, Cedic and Isanovic, were called out of the room by two paramilitary men who said that dynamite had been found in their homes." You did not mention any guards; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: FWS-73 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again I have to point out, all lists for anyone came from the camp administration, then this is read out. We were there, we the inmates, and when that name is read out, that name goes out and then it says that in the case of that name a radio transmitter was found, weapons were found, whatever. In their case specifically, it was said that lots of dynamite was found. So the others who came in -- I think that's just the way it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: You did not mention any guards here or lists. You mentioned two members of the paramilitary units. "Two members of paramilitary units called out his name and took him out of the room." Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: FWS-73 [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is correct. However, the list, I repeat again, that they got it and that they worked according to that list.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: How come you know where they got that list from?

utterances.speaker: FWS-73 [Resumed]
utterances.text: How come I know where they got that list from? The entrance door into the camp, no one can pass it, either from the inside or from the outside, without being seen.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: So in this specific case, you saw that somebody passed through the door and had a list. Who was this?

utterances.speaker: FWS-73 [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as the list is concerned, they got either in the yard or in the administration.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Where did these two members of the paramilitary units get their lists, specifically?

utterances.speaker: FWS-73 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am telling you that every list they got, they got from the administration of the camp because, again I repeat, they did not know any of the inmates.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. I'm asking you about a specific case. Did you see who were -- who from, when and where they got that list? I'm asking you about the incident concerning Cedic and Isanovic specifically.

utterances.speaker: FWS-73 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I repeat -- I've been repeating this for several times now. Extremists who were at the camp would read this and say the following: "Who is Isanovic?" And then he would say, "It's me." "Who is Cedic?" That's what I've been telling you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Thank you. Where were you that morning when the war conflict broke out in Foca?

utterances.speaker: FWS-73 [Resumed]
utterances.text: When the war conflict broke out in Foca, I was at my business establishment. On that day, we started to work. I've been repeating this several times as well. When I saw the Serb population, people I knew, I saw them going somewhere, going en masse, I was wondering what's all this about? And not three hours had gone by when the shooting started.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Who were you with? Could you just wait for the interpretation, please?

utterances.speaker: FWS-73 [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the moment when the war broke out, I, my wife, and the girl who worked at our place were there.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Are you sure you were not in the cafe near the Cafe Bor and drinking coffee with friends?

utterances.speaker: FWS-73 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Coffee? I did have coffee on that day, in a coffee bar owned by (redacted) and that coffee bar (redacted). That area is called Prijeka Carsija, in the centre of the old town (redacted) (redacted).

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: I'm now going to read to you what you said to the investigators of the OTP in your first statement: "The shooting started around 9.00 in the morning and lasted for about three hours. At that time, I was in a small restaurant and drinking coffee with my friends."

utterances.speaker: FWS-73 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't see -- I mean I just didn't mention the owner of that shop, whose name is (redacted).

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: So you were not near the Cafe Bor?

utterances.speaker: FWS-73 [Resumed]
utterances.text: (redacted)

utterances.speaker: FWS-73 [Resumed]
utterances.text: (redacted).

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Are you sure that you did not say in any one of your statements that you were having coffee near the Cafe Bor?

utterances.speaker: FWS-73 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I repeat -- I have my own witnesses for everything I've been saying before this Honourable Court. I repeat: As I was leaving the camp, I gave those statements. If anyone had written anything to me, just like in the camp, I would have signed it.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Where were your children on that day when the war broke out in Foca?

utterances.speaker: FWS-73 [Resumed]
utterances.text: When the war broke out in Foca, my children were spending the weekend 33 kilometres away. The town is called Gorazde.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Spending the weekend there, where, with whom?

utterances.speaker: FWS-73 [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were visiting with my sister, my only sister, and her husband and her children.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Do you know what day this was when the conflict broke out?

utterances.speaker: FWS-73 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think in my opinion, that it was the first day after the weekend.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: You said that they had left for the weekend?

utterances.speaker: FWS-73 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: And the first day after the weekend, they were not there?

utterances.speaker: FWS-73 [Resumed]
utterances.text: They went away for the weekend. And let me tell the Honourable Court the other thing. These same children went to Novi Sad when they heard that everything was burning over here and that it was being torched. They went to stay with their grandmother.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Thank you. Yesterday, you mentioned that with Arso Krnojelac, a driver of the KP Dom, you drove barrels to Zavajt. Who were you taking these barrels to?

utterances.speaker: FWS-73 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yesterday - and also today I'm saying it before this Honourable Court - I said -- I spoke of one barrel only, not barrels. We took this barrel from this barrel man who made -- who made these barrels by the Serb cemetery in Foca.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: And who did you take it to in Zavajt?

utterances.speaker: FWS-73 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That barrel was something that we had to take because we were going to load wood in Zavajt anyway, so that barrel was loaded by the driver of the freight vehicle. His last name is also Krnojelac and it's only then that I found out that he was Krnojelac's brother.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Sir, it was my understanding yesterday that you said that you unloaded that barrel in Zavajt in front of the house. In front of whose house?

utterances.speaker: FWS-73 [Resumed]
utterances.text: We unloaded that barrel -- I mean, Krnojelac's brother said that it was his barrel, and we unloaded it in front of the house. And I did not know exactly, because Krnojelac and his brother moved into Foca. He unloaded it there in front of the house, and I thought that it was his house because he said that it was his barrel.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. All of this related to the barrel, I mean, what you heard. You said that the barrel was unloaded. Who did Arso Krnojelac talk to when he said that he was telling his brother not to take that duty upon him?

utterances.speaker: FWS-73 [Resumed]
utterances.text: A villager - I mean, after we unloaded that barrel - talked to Krnojelac's brother. And we were waiting for this conversation to end because we did not dare do anything without orders. We personally heard this conversation.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: You don't have to repeat all of this. You said all of this yesterday. I was just wondering whether you had remembered all of it.

utterances.speaker: FWS-73 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Are you sure that there is only one Krnojelac house in Zavajt?

utterances.speaker: FWS-73 [Resumed]
utterances.text: In response to your question -- I mean, I answered your question before that. All the people who came from the vicinity -- I mean, until the present day, I do not know -- until the present day, I do not know which village they are from.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Sir, you gave three statements to the Office of the Prosecutor and one to the security station in Sarajevo. Why did you not mention this in a single statement that you had given? Did you remember this only nine years later?

utterances.speaker: FWS-73 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me explain something to you in relation to this question. This didn't mean a thing to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: And why did it mean something to you yesterday?

utterances.speaker: FWS-73 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me explain this to you. You are asking me about every single detail, so I have to concentrate so hard that I have to answer whatever you are asking me to answer in relation to every little detail.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: The witness had actually talked about this incident before in a statement given to the Prosecutor's Office, and it's a statement given on the 16th and 18th December 1998, where he was questioned about Krnojelac particularly, and in the last paragraph, he actually mentions this incident. He doesn't speak about this village as such but about the incident.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: You mean with the barrel.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: And has that been given to the Defence?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I don't want the Prosecutor to understand this as criticism, but I got that statement only yesterday, just before this witness came in, for the very first time. Secondly, it was not presented in the same form as the witness had put it here. I'm going to read it out to him, and in my opinion, this is not the same statement. With your permission, let this be my question as well, and at the same time, this may be an explanation of what I have been telling you what this statement actually says. "After Krnojelac went to prison, his older brother, who was a driver in the prison, he talked to other detainees on the truck. I do not remember who was there any more, but I remember that he criticised his brother about what had happened in KP Dom because he accepted the post of commander of the prison." I don't know how he mentioned a barrel in Zavajt or talking to a Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. person from that village. There's been no mention of that here. Secondly, the witness said that at the time, Milorad Krnojelac was the warden. So I don't want to identify his testimony now as something that had already been put in the same way previously.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Well, Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff, there doesn't seem to be any reference to a barrel there. There is a reference to a truck. It's a shame it's the first time Mr. Bakrac has actually got to one of the facts of the case rather than completely irrelevant inconsistencies, but he may have a point. There doesn't seem to be anything in the statement that talks about the barrel and being delivered to the brother's house.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, this reference in this statement is rather brief, and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: It may be, but it was a fair enough thing to put to the witness. That's what I'm putting to you. There is no reference in the statement to what the witness has told us in Court.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, then I have to apologise. To me it was clear that this is the reference.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Well, it's certainly not clear to me. You proceed, Mr. Bakrac.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Before you do, there are different ways of cross-examining on inconsistencies, but as a matter of ordinary human experience, no court could ever expect a witness to say something in exactly the same way in a statement as he does when he gives his evidence. You would be rather suspicious if they did. The inconsistencies, however, may be quite marked, but the question then arises: Is the inconsistency in relation to something which we have to decide? Certainly if a witness has got a whole string of statements in his evidence which are inconsistent with what he had told the OTP's investigators, you might think that he's reckless or something like that. But where his children were and whether he'd had coffee and that sort of stuff doesn't seem, to me, to give us any idea as to whether or not this man is telling the truth about what we are here to decide. We're not here to decide whether he had coffee or whether he didn't have coffee or whether he had it at one cafe or another. We're here to consider what he's telling us about and that is the beatings and the killings inside the KP Dom. Now, if he's got inconsistencies about that, we would be far more interested than we would about these what I would describe as quite irrelevant details. So I may suggest to you that you concentrate, if there are such inconsistencies, that you concentrate on them. We will get along a lot more quickly and have a lot less problems with the witness' answers.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, by your leave, can we have an explanation? I think it is necessary for me to explain something. The questions related to children and coffee are not put by way of an inconsistency. The Prosecutor referred to the transcript of Witness 33, and we accepted this, and the Prosecutor has dwelt on this extensively, that Serb families sent their children out of Foca, expecting what would happen to happen. So that is what the Defence wanted to do, to point to the reasons why the witness' children were not there. In addition to that, we have lots of information that by the Cafe Bor, there was a Muslim barricade where the shooting actually started. Then also the Defence has reason to believe - I will say this quite clearly - that this witness took part in what happened at the barricade, in the shooting, and that is why I put the questions related to the children and to the barricade and the coffee, and I felt it necessary to give this explanation to you as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: I can only hope that you will get to that issue. If you want to raise that issue about whether he was a combattant rather than a civilian, you go to that, but let's get there, please. You can see yourself that this witness is not easy to keep on the track. He doesn't answer the questions. So let's keep to the relevant questions and see if we can keep him on track on those.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Sir, we've already said this, so there is no reason for me not to ask you that. Were you at the roadblock near the Cafe Bor in Donje Polje?

utterances.speaker: FWS-73 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I say about myself that I was no political figure, that I was not a member of any party, and even those extremists verified that and saw that, and nevertheless, I thought now this is the end of me, like all the others.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: I asked you a specific question. Were you at the roadblock near Cafe Bor?

utterances.speaker: FWS-73 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was on no roadblock. I never took part in any meetings.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Thank you. Yesterday, you said, sir, that you had seen Mr. Maksimovic with Krnojelac in the KP Dom, towards the end of your detention, that you saw them walking towards the furniture factory. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: FWS-73 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am telling the Honourable Court that I cannot exactly quote the dates, but Maksimovic, Ostojic, Cancar --

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Sir --

utterances.speaker: FWS-73 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me answer this question: -- were coming, and he was coming out because nothing could happen in the prison compound without having to do with the warden, Savo Todovic, Rasevic, and the others. In other words, he was with him when that furniture was taken out. Our men loaded it.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Who was with him?

utterances.speaker: FWS-73 [Resumed]
utterances.text: With him was the warden.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Which warden?

utterances.speaker: FWS-73 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's common knowledge who the warden is.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Tell us his name?

utterances.speaker: FWS-73 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Milorad Krnojelac. Everything that went on in the camp --

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Sir --

utterances.speaker: FWS-73 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, no. I must repeat a hundred times, a hundred times. I must repeat this. I told the Honourable Court yesterday everything that goes into the compound goes through the administration, and therefore I do not wish to answer any such provocations any more.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Look, sir, there was a very simple question. You were asked to tell us his name. You gave his name. Now, there was nothing that you needed to add to that. If you just answer the question, we will get along a lot more quickly and you will do far better in your evidence if you will stick to the questions and answer those alone. Yes, Mr. Bakrac.

utterances.speaker: FWS-73 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I understand, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Sir, you saw Krnojelac with him, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: FWS-73 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Now I shall read to you what you told the OTP in your first statement of 1995. And for the interpreters, it is page 5, the first statement, October 1995, document marked 138A and passage before -- one passage, the penultimate passage, last one on that: "I saw Maksimovic once in the KP Dom, towards the end of my imprisonment, as he walked towards the furniture factory with several other men, about whom I heard later that they were a delegation from Serbia. I do not know what -- why were they -- why were they in the prison." Now, what is correct? Which one of your statements is correct?

utterances.speaker: FWS-73 [Resumed]
utterances.text: When you say "delegation," before the Honourable Court, I never once spoke about no delegation. I spoke about extremists. There was an extremist group which came, and all that is true.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Do you mean that the OTP simply did not take down your statement correctly?

utterances.speaker: FWS-73 [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I said -- when I gave my statement in Sarajevo, that I signed it, just like when I was in the camp in Foca.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: This is not a statement from the public security centre in Sarajevo. This is a statement that you gave to the OTP in October, 1995.

utterances.speaker: FWS-73 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I mention it now, and I repeat, I spent two and a half years in that camp, and now you want me to say there was so and so, and so and so. Whilst I did see those people, those people who were even greater extremists than those in the camp, and every visit had to do with the warden and his team, and I don't want to repeat it any more.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: But is that part of the statement correct when you said that it was towards the end of your imprisonment?

utterances.speaker: FWS-73 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that the dates, I can't -- towards the end of my departure, because towards the end of my departure, Zoran Sekulovic was the warden of the camp.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: So it is true that it was towards the end of your imprisonment?

utterances.speaker: FWS-73 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I say it was towards the end of my imprisonment, and towards the end of my imprisonment Zoran Sekulovic was the camp warden. I repeat it again. So this happened before that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: When did you leave the prison?

utterances.speaker: FWS-73 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I left the prison on the 10th of October, 1994.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: So did this, what you mentioned here, happen in 1994?

utterances.speaker: FWS-73 [Resumed]
utterances.text: This, perhaps. I cannot remember the date, but I know that the furniture factory started to operate shortly, not long -- it did not take long for the furniture factory to start its operation, which means that Zoran Sekulovic was not a warden then.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Do you still stand by that you saw Krnojelac with Maksimovic, or are you inferring -- are you making this inference because you say that nothing could be done without the administration? Will you -- will you please answer concretely? Did you see him with Maksimovic or was that your conjecture because nothing could be done without the administrator?

utterances.speaker: FWS-73 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm telling the truth to the Honourable Court. It happened, I repeat, when Zoran Sekulovic - Zoran Pljevaljcic, is he Pljevaljcic? - was not the warden. It happened in Krnojelac -- in Milorad Krnojelac's time, who was the warden of the camp. And when Maksimovic turned up, everything would run -- whenever Maksimovic appeared, everybody would run out to greet him. Now, what it was about, I did not -- it didn't really matter to me because I could only try to make myself scarce, to make myself invisible in the yard. But I know it was in Krnojelac's time and I am confident that he was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: So you did not see him; you are confident?

utterances.speaker: FWS-73 [Resumed]
utterances.text: My today's conviction, that is. I am convicted today, which means that I saw him and that it cannot be that I did not see him.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Did you, in any of your previous statements to the OTP, mention that you did some work on Milorad Krnojelac's house?

utterances.speaker: FWS-73 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Who did you make this statement to?

utterances.speaker: FWS-73 [Resumed]
utterances.text: All the statements that I gave, let me tell you, under a code number.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: I don't understand. You made coded statements?

utterances.speaker: FWS-73 [Resumed]
utterances.text: All the statements that I gave and to whom I gave those statements, the Honourable Court has it.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: And you're claiming that in those statements you spoke about the work that you did on Krnojelac's house, that it is in your statements?

utterances.speaker: FWS-73 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Whether it is written down -- maybe it is not written down, but I say that I worked there, before the Honourable Court.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Does that mean that you did not read any one of those statements nor were your statements read to you?

utterances.speaker: FWS-73 [Resumed]
utterances.text: My statements, what I stated, were accessible to me, except when I was in the camp in Sarajevo, not one was accessible to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Then why this important detail about how you worked on Krnojelac's house, rather, on Krnojelac's coffee shop, why is it that we don't find that important detail in any one of your statements?

utterances.speaker: FWS-73 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I repeat before the Honourable Court. My yesterday's testimony which I made before the Honourable Court was that I had worked in a coffee shop which is in the camp warden's house, that I worked in the shop to be owned by Saja Sahimpasic. Before the Court I said it yesterday. If I have to repeat it again, tell me.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: He's not asking you whether you said it yesterday or not. He's asking you: Did you tell the OTP's investigators? Is it in your statement anywhere? Now, he's entitled to ask you that. And it's not an answer by saying, "What I said in Court yesterday was true." Now, please, do you say that you told the investigators about having worked in Mr. Krnojelac's house? Now, you can answer that "Yes," or "No," or "I don't remember."

utterances.speaker: FWS-73 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've said it.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, perhaps I should move on, because I think the answer is quite clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Tell us, where is that Sahimpasic's shop that you tell us he took over?

utterances.speaker: FWS-73 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Saja Sahimpasic's shop is in front of the department store in Foca. It is the only department store in Foca, and it is call Focanka.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Yesterday, you told the Court how you had a transistor radio in the KP Dom; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: FWS-73 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Did you have it throughout your detention?

utterances.speaker: FWS-73 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The transistor was hidden so that if the guards were to find it, we'd be beaten and killed, so that we kept hiding it.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Did you have it throughout your detention?

utterances.speaker: FWS-73 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No way.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Does that mean that the guards found the transistor?

utterances.speaker: FWS-73 [Resumed]
utterances.text: They found the transistor.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Did they punish you because of that?

utterances.speaker: FWS-73 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Jasmin Sudar was beaten, battered, and killed because allegedly he had it. Who had said that he had it, I don't know, but he was beaten, battered, and killed and disappeared.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Did you mention him yesterday? Why didn't you mention this incident yesterday?

utterances.speaker: FWS-73 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Do you know how many of such incidents happened? Hundreds and hundreds of them. I'd have to be a computer to really drag them out of my head.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: But tell us, sir, was it a power- or battery-operated transistor?

utterances.speaker: FWS-73 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was battery operated.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: And how did you obtain batteries?

utterances.speaker: FWS-73 [Resumed]
utterances.text: You ask how we obtain batteries. I mentioned before the Honourable Court that it used to be the penitentiary reformatory before the war, a Yugoslav one, so that there were still clothes left over, transistors, batteries, and as I mentioned, there were also sheepskins for officers, as we had to call them, and the like.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Where was it left behind, in the storeroom or where?

utterances.speaker: FWS-73 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The storerooms of the KP Dom, and they were wide open.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: And you could simply walk in and take whatever you needed?

utterances.speaker: FWS-73 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I, who worked everywhere -- and that is why I was surprised yesterday when I pointed with this stick to the Honourable Court, when I showed -- when I pointed the canteen rather than the offices because I didn't have my glasses. All of the locales which there were from the furniture factory to its offices, to the canteen, to the canteen offices, every -- I know where every detail is and how it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Thank you. Which station were you tuned in on that radio?

utterances.speaker: FWS-73 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The station that we listened to was Radio Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: And Radio Foca? No?

utterances.speaker: FWS-73 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Radio Foca was listened to when it was accessible to me up there at Brioni, that is, at Brioni farm, because up there there were several Serbs who had been detained and worked up there, and they had the right to listen to the Foca Radio, and we listened to it for a while. Afterwards Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. it was prohibited.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: And Radio Sarajevo you could hear in the KP Dom?

utterances.speaker: FWS-73 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Barely, just barely.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: And which station was it that you heard that they assigned various business outlets to combattants?

utterances.speaker: FWS-73 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I said before the Honourable Court that on a Serb station, that is, Foca Radio, which existed before the war too, at the farm, which is 3 kilometres away and which was also part of the camp, and I also pointed out that the radio announcer -- and perhaps I did not explain it with all the details, but he said that business outlets are granted in Foca. The advantage is accorded to Serb combattants. And we know the Serb combattants who had committed a sin against that people, that in the early days they were the principal butchers and the greatest Vojvodas as proven by the fact that in front of the department store, business outlets are run by Chetnik Vojvodas who had escaped from Foca.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: And was it the same radio that you heard that Adnan Isanovic and two or three more people had been killed?

utterances.speaker: FWS-73 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The radio that we had in our rooms - I mentioned it yesterday before the Honourable Court - that there was a woman of Serb origin who reported, and Semso Tucakovic, a journalist, received those reports. And everything that went on in Foca in those early days, we learned all about that, about all the killings and everything, and that was not accessible to us.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: And you heard it from Semso Tucakovic on the radio; is it?

utterances.speaker: FWS-73 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, on the transistor. He said who was his source and how he came by that information. We learned that Serb extremists had captured that individual and that that individual had fared like hundreds and hundreds of our folk.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: You also said that the guards in the KP Dom told you about all the ill-treatment and murders; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: FWS-73 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I always stand by those, except not all. A couple of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: They would come to you and tell you who killed whom, who beat whom, is that it?

utterances.speaker: FWS-73 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm now saying before the Honourable Court how the lawyer concerned is provoking my replies with his supposed great knowledge before the Honourable Court. He's begun to provoke me. Before this Honourable Court, I, in my yesterday's testimony, wrote two or three names who told us about all the people who committed misdeeds in that compound, and I don't want to repeat it again.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: I did not provoke you. You've just told us that they informed -- that they had informed you. That was my question.

utterances.speaker: FWS-73 [Resumed]
utterances.text: My answer is yes, and I repeated it yesterday and today, and I don't know how many times I'll have to repeat it again.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Do you know a guard called Risto Ivanovic?

utterances.speaker: FWS-73 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know him very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: And what kind of a guard was he?

utterances.speaker: FWS-73 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I -- it is embarrassing for me to say that. That is, it is not embarrassing to tell before the Honourable Court, but these details - and I'm speaking from my point of view, to tell you - had I known yesterday that you would lay your hands on those men, I wouldn't answer that, because now you ask me about a man who was -- I can't explain anything to you, because, had they all been the same, I wouldn't be sitting here today. That is my answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: The question was what sort of a guard was he. Can you not answer that question?

utterances.speaker: FWS-73 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I say to the Honourable Court, and I repeat: If I say here what kind of a man was he -- I've just said, had they all been the same, we would have disappeared, but I am referring to him because he's asking me about him. That is my answer, if he got it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Is it your attitude, then -- and I'm not criticising you for it, I just want to know, is it your attitude, then, that you will not discuss any guard who is named in court? Is that so?

utterances.speaker: FWS-73 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I dare not speak about people of goodwill, and who were -- who, as our folk say, who had committed no sin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: If the name had been written down on a piece of paper, would you be prepared to explain what sort of a guard he was, so that the name was not revealed in public?

utterances.speaker: FWS-73 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know, but as far as -- as I know about law, I can write the name down for the Honourable Court but not for the lawyer. The lawyer should not be told that because I know that extremist groups still wield power there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Well, sir, if that is your attitude, it's no use proceeding with this particular type of inquiry because you can't tell us anything that the Defence counsel is not also told. There you are, Mr. Bakrac. I think you should get on to some other issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Yes, I agree. I will move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Were there any Serbs in the KP Dom when you arrived? Did you find them there when you arrived, people who had been imprisoned there before the war conflict, who had been convicts serving their terms?

utterances.speaker: FWS-73 [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were a few of them. I don't know how it happened that they had been left behind.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Thank you. And where were those persons kept?

utterances.speaker: FWS-73 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those persons were up at the farm, and then later on, some of them came down to the camp, but they had a room of their own downstairs on the ground floor. Allegedly those told them to leave, to go, but they seemed reluctant. They said, "Well, I will, I won't," and so I suppose they were telling them to go to the front line.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Yesterday, you said that the guard had told you that if somebody saw you talking to him without him beating you, that he'd be immediately sent to the front line. Is that it?

utterances.speaker: FWS-73 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Do you still go by this or can you tell us which guard told you that?

utterances.speaker: FWS-73 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Once again, before the Honourable Court, I don't know if I'm all that difficult to understand but I wrote this for the Honourable Court. If you didn't remember that name, then I'm not going to write it today again. So you forgot his name? Well, I'm glad you did.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Well, perhaps my memory is not as good as yours but you wrote down two names yesterday.

utterances.speaker: FWS-73 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, then, I'm saying -- I apologise to the Honourable Court that I have to repeat it again, so you non-stop -- you keep asking me the same questions time and time again. So you want me again -- well, I will write them but only for the Honourable Court. I don't want you to get them.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
